CausalChain: Tumor cells -> secretion of EVs enriched in specific miRNAs (e.g., miR-21, miR-155) and cytokines -> uptake by mature myeloid cells -> downregulation of IRF-8 and C/EBPα -> aberrant differentiation into MDSCs -> accumulation of immunosuppressive MDSCs -> enhanced T cell inhibition and tumor immune escape
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry specific miRNAs, such as miR-21 and miR-155, whose delivery—enhanced by a supporting cytokine milieu—leads to the downregulation of critical myeloid differentiation transcription factors IRF-8 and C/EBPα in mature myeloid cells. This molecular event redirects their differentiation, promoting the formation and accumulation of immunosuppressive MDSCs. We further hypothesize that contemporary molecular techniques, including single-cell RNA-sequencing and CRISPR-based screens, can elucidate this EV-miRNA mediated reprogramming mechanism. Moreover, using engineered EVs or miRNA antagonists to disrupt the EV-miRNA axis offers a promising therapeutic intervention to restore normal myeloid differentiation and enhance cancer immunotherapy response.
Abstract: We propose that tumor cells not only secrete extracellular vesicles (EVs) enriched in specific microRNAs – including candidate miRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-155 – but also create a cytokine-rich microenvironment that synergistically facilitates the reprogramming of myeloid cells. Upon uptake of these EVs by mature myeloid cells, the delivered miRNAs, in concert with tumor-derived cytokine signals, downregulate key transcription factors IRF-8 and C/EBPα. This dual regulatory mechanism perturbs normal myeloid differentiation, promoting a phenotypic shift toward immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and culminating in enhanced T cell inhibition and tumor immune escape. Leveraging cutting-edge technologies such as single-cell RNA-sequencing and CRISPR-based functional screens, along with engineered EVs for targeted miRNA antagonism, our approach offers a novel therapeutic strategy to restore proper myeloid differentiation and improve the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original concept that tumor-derived EVs deliver miRNAs which suppress IRF-8 and C/EBPα, leading to an MDSC phenotype and subsequent immune evasion. However, it now explicitly integrates candidate miRNAs (e.g., miR-21, miR-155) and incorporates the synergistic role of tumor-derived cytokines, which address concerns over the mechanistic clarity of the conversion process. Additionally, leveraging modern technologies like single-cell RNA-seq and CRISPR screening, as well as proposing engineered EVs for targeted intervention, enhances the practical implementability and experimental tractability of the hypothesis. Each step of the original causal chain is maintained and expanded: from secretion of EVs, their uptake and suppression of transcription factors, to the consequent MDSC accumulation and immune suppression, thereby offering a more detailed and testable framework.
